sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- lens_diagnostics: lens_diagnostics source=session reads the session cache and an empty cache is not proof of a clean file; use source=lsp scope=paths for changed files when cached findings are absent or stale
- symbol_search: Find files by identifier
- effective_config: Explain resolved configuration
- project_report: Orient in a project before choosing a file
- module_report: Outline a source module before reading a body
- read_symbol: Read one symbol's body instead of the whole file
- read_enclosing: Read the enclosing symbol or callback body for a line
- pi_lens_activate_tools: Activate a situational tool
- subagent_gate: Run subagent tasks with bounded retries and a required success quorum
- workspace_session_summaries: Inspect same-CWD session summaries before potentially overlapping repository work
- subagent: Delegate focused work to child agents; compose multi-child work in one workflow call.
- subagents_enable: pi-subagents is installed. For authorized specialist, independent-review, or parallel work, call subagents_enable, then subagent. Authorization must come from the current request or applicable instructions; complexity alone is not authorization.
- ask_user_question: Ask the user up to 4 structured questions (2-4 options each) when requirements are ambiguous
- workflow: Delegate substantive independent or staged work to subagents with a JavaScript workflow, optionally composing agent calls with parallel(), pipeline(), or both
- workflow_control: Inspect and manage workflow runs directly by canonical run ID.

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use subagent_gate instead of raw subagent calls when a delegated result must be retried safely or a success quorum must be enforced.
- Set each subagent_gate task retrySafety to read-only only when rerunning it cannot duplicate file mutations or external side effects; omission defaults to may-write.
- Use workspace_session_summaries when another Pi session in the same working directory may overlap the current work.
- After workspace_session_summaries, compare goals, files or symbols, decisions, and next steps; when overlap is material or ownership is unclear, coordinate through intercom before writing.
- Use ask_user_question whenever the user's request is underspecified and you cannot proceed without concrete decisions — you can ask up to 4 questions per invocation.
- Each question MUST have 2-4 options. Every option requires a concise label (1-5 words) and a description explaining what the choice means or its trade-offs. The user can additionally type a custom answer via the automatically appended "Type something." row on every question, or press Esc to abandon the questionnaire. Do NOT author "Other" or "Type something." labels yourself — reserved labels are rejected at runtime.
- Set multiSelect: true when multiple answers are valid. Provide an options[].preview markdown string when an option benefits from richer side-by-side context (mockups, code snippets, diagrams, configs) — single-select only. The "Type something." row is appended to every question; in preview mode it expands to the full pane width while typing so the custom answer is not cramped into the narrow options column. If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option and append "(Recommended)" to its label.
- Do not stack multiple ask_user_question calls back-to-back — group all clarifying questions into one invocation.
- The `workflow` tool runs multi-agent orchestration — it fans decomposable work out across subagents, and fits tasks shaped like: repo-wide inspection, independent parallel research/checks, multi-perspective review, or fan-out/fan-in synthesis. ONLY call it when the user explicitly opts in — via the workflow trigger word, `/workflows run`, or their own words (e.g. 'run a workflow', 'fan this out', '并行审一遍'). For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit — do not call it; you may briefly offer it (with a rough cost) as an option instead.
- Use workflow_control for workflow lifecycle management; do not ask the user to type /workflows when this tool can perform the action.
- Use stop to terminate or quit a run. Closing the navigator does not stop a run.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: timeout_evaluate
toolsAdded.description: Evaluate whether a long-running command should be terminated or allowed to continue. Called by the agent in response to a timeout alert.

toolCallId.description: The toolCallId of the bash command being evaluated

terminate.description: Whether to terminate the command (true) or allow it to continue (false)

toolsAdded.name: fail_stage
toolsAdded.description: Report a stage failure or review rejection with a structured reason. KainBain will route the task back to the stage configured for failback on this stage — do not specify or request a target stage yourself.

reason.description: Detailed reason why the stage failed or why the work was rejected

toolsAdded.name: browser
toolsAdded.description:
Browser automation via agent-browser CLI.
Workflow: open URL → snapshot -i (get @refs like @e1) → interact → re-snapshot after page changes.
Commands:
  open <url> - Navigate to URL
  snapshot -i - Interactive elements with @refs (re-snapshot after navigation)
  click <@ref> - Click element
  fill <@ref> <text> - Clear and type
  type <@ref> <text> - Type without clearing
  select <@ref> <value> - Select dropdown
  press <key> - Press key (Enter, Tab, etc.)
  scroll <dir> [px] - Scroll (up/down/left/right)
  get text|url|title [@ref] - Get information
  wait <@ref|ms> - Wait for element or time
  screenshot [--full] - Take screenshot (image returned inline)
  close - Close browser
Any valid agent-browser command works.

toolsAdded.name: browser_open
toolsAdded.description: Launch a managed Chromium tab or securely attach to a loopback CDP browser.

target.description: URL substring when attaching to CDP

toolsAdded.name: browser_navigate
toolsAdded.description: Navigate a named browser tab and invalidate old element refs.

toolsAdded.name: browser_observe
toolsAdded.description: Return current interactive elements with stable refs. Use those refs with browser_act.

toolsAdded.name: browser_act
toolsAdded.description: Click, fill, press, hover, select, scroll, wait, screenshot, or upload using a selector or browser_observe ref.

toolsAdded.name: browser_run
toolsAdded.description: Evaluate JavaScript in the active page. Use browser_observe and browser_act for normal automation.

toolsAdded.name: browser_events
toolsAdded.description: Read persistent console, failed-request, and HTTP-error events for a tab.

toolsAdded.name: browser_tabs
toolsAdded.description: List named automation tabs.

toolsAdded.name: browser_select
toolsAdded.description: Select a page in a CDP-attached browser by URL substring.

toolsAdded.name: browser_close
toolsAdded.description: Close one named tab or all automation tabs. CDP mode disconnects without closing the user browser.

toolsAdded.name: lens_diagnostics
toolsAdded.description: Query pi-lens diagnostics from the session cache or an active LSP probe, at paths or workspace scope. Empty cache is not proof of clean; probe changed paths when findings are absent or stale. Example: `{source: "lsp", scope: "paths", paths: ["src/app.ts"]}`.

source.description: Evidence source: session cache (empty cache is not proof of a clean file — use source=lsp for changed files) or an active LSP probe.

scope.description: Coverage scope: explicit paths, or workspace (default: current turn's delta for source=session).

mode.description: delta = current turn; all = cache-only; full = active LSP scan of paths. Empty cache is not proof of clean.

path.description: One file or directory for source=lsp checks.

waitMs.description: Source=lsp per-file wait budget in milliseconds.

serverScope.description: Source=lsp server coverage: primary or all.

refreshRunners.description: Analyzer refresh mode for full view.

maxLspFiles.description: File limit for the LSP sweep.

includeGenerated.description: Include generated-name paths in full scans.

analysisRoot.description: Explicit project directory for heavyweight analyzers; it must exist and resolve strictly below the home directory.

severity.description: Filter by severity threshold (default: all): error shows errors; warning includes errors and warnings; information includes errors, warnings, and information; hint and all show every known tier.

toolsAdded.name: symbol_search
toolsAdded.description: Find relevant files by ranked identifier search. On a cold cache, project_report and symbol_search return available: false with a retry hint and start a non-blocking background build; module_report degrades to outline-only with cache freshness explicit. Example: search `authenticate user` before module_report.

query.description: Identifier-ish query, e.g. 'authenticate user'. Mix in composable prefix filters: lang:<kind> (e.g. lang:jsts, lang:python — kinds from file-kinds.ts), file:<substr> (path substring), ext:<ext> (e.g. ext:ts or ext:.ts), each optionally negated with a leading '-' (-file:test). Filters apply before ranking; e.g. 'lang:jsts file:clients/ -file:test rank'. Unknown prefixes/kinds error with the supported list.

paths.description: Glob array scoping hits to matching files — same shape/semantics as ast_grep_search's `paths` (a bare directory/file entry scopes its whole subtree). Filters before ranking, so scores within the scoped set are unaffected.

lang.description: Restrict hits to one language, using the same identifiers as ast_grep_search's `lang` param (e.g. 'typescript', 'python', 'go').

toolsAdded.name: effective_config
toolsAdded.description: Explain resolved configuration and provenance. Response is redacted by construction: it contains no environment values, no command arguments beyond the binary, and home-relative paths; a tier-denied LSP decision cannot be lifted by a nearer config. Example: pass `file` to see why its LSP server is selected.

file.description: Path to explain: adds the resolved language plus the per-server and per-runner selection decisions for it. Must resolve inside `cwd` (a sibling package in the same monorepo does not count) — a file outside it is rejected with the `cwd` it was measured against; re-query with `cwd` set to that file's own workspace instead.

toolsAdded.name: project_report
toolsAdded.description: Orient in a project from its review graph, with ranked hubs and entry points. On a cold cache, project_report and symbol_search return available: false with a retry hint and start a non-blocking background build; module_report degrades to outline-only with cache freshness explicit. Example: use project_report before module_report when the target file is unknown.

limit.description: Scales every ranked section's cap (default 10) — a single knob for all sections.

focus.description: Optional task hint used only to re-rank sections toward relevant subsystems (does not expand scope or trigger scans).

view.description: Payload tier. compact (cheapest) returns a line-oriented TEXT rendering instead of JSON. Default returns JSON.

toolsAdded.name: module_report
toolsAdded.description: Return a navigable source-module outline with symbols, references, and read handles. An outline shows shape, not bodies, and does not satisfy read-before-edit; `read_symbol` and `read_enclosing` return body text and record read coverage. On a cold cache, project_report and symbol_search return available: false with a retry hint and start a non-blocking background build; module_report degrades to outline-only with cache freshness explicit. Example: use module_report on `src/app.ts` before read_symbol.

maxRefsPerSymbol.description: Cap on who-uses-this entries per symbol (default 10).

focus.description: Optional task hint used only to rank recommendedReads (does not expand scope or trigger scans).

view.description: Payload tier. summary returns top-level entries/recommendedReads and section provenance with heavy callback/usedBy/blast-radius payloads omitted. compact (cheapest) returns a line-oriented TEXT rendering of the full report instead of JSON.

blastRadius.description: Include the cross-file blast-radius section: transitive dependents aggregated to ranked file reads. Read-only over the cached graph (omitted when cold).

blastRadiusDepth.description: Max hops for the blast-radius walk (default 3). Only used with blastRadius.

callGraph.description: Include bounded derived callers/callees from the cached FunctionCallGraph; cold or stale cache state is explicit.

toolsAdded.name: read_symbol
toolsAdded.description: Return one symbol's verbatim source. An outline shows shape, not bodies, and does not satisfy read-before-edit; `read_symbol` and `read_enclosing` return body text and record read coverage. Example: use read_symbol after module_report identifies `parseConfig`.

path.description: Absolute or workspace-relative path to the source file.

symbol.description: Exact symbol name or callback handle to read (e.g. a function, class, type, or module_report callbacks[].name). Accepts a dotted `Class.method` name to resolve a member.

kind.description: Optional kind filter (e.g. function, interface, class) to disambiguate when multiple same-file symbols share the requested name. Omitting it returns the first match, same as today.

toolsAdded.name: read_enclosing
toolsAdded.description: Return the smallest symbol or callback enclosing a line. An outline shows shape, not bodies, and does not satisfy read-before-edit; `read_symbol` and `read_enclosing` return body text and record read coverage. Example: use read_enclosing after a diagnostic points to line 42.

path.description: Absolute or workspace-relative path to the source file.

line.description: 1-based line number inside the desired symbol/callback.

kinds.description: Optional kind filter, e.g. function, method, callback, class, object_property_callback.

maxLines.description: Optional maximum body size to return. Oversized matches obey onOversize.

onOversize.description: Behavior when the enclosing body exceeds maxLines. error (default) returns metadata only; slice returns a bounded partial read around line; outline returns nested symbols/callbacks with read handles.

aroundLine.description: Maximum lines for onOversize=slice; defaults to maxLines, then 80.

toolsAdded.name: pi_lens_activate_tools
toolsAdded.description: Activate registered situational tools for the next turn. Example: `{tools: ["ast_grep_search"]}`.

tools.description: Names of situational tools to activate, e.g. `ast_grep_search`.

toolsAdded.name: goal_complete
toolsAdded.description: Mark an active /goal complete only when the latest effective Goal contract explicitly says Goal mode is active, supplies the matching current goal_id, and every requirement is verified. Tool visibility alone does not activate Goal mode. Never call for ordinary work, partial progress, blockers, failures, or unverified work.

goal_id.description: The exact goal_id shown in the current active /goal prompt. Used only to reject stale completion calls from older turns.

summary.description: State what was completed and what evidence verified it. Do not use this tool to report partial progress, blockers, failures, or remaining work.

toolsAdded.name: goal_blocked
toolsAdded.description: Stop an active /goal only when the latest effective Goal contract explicitly says Goal mode is active, supplies the matching current goal_id, and the same evidenced external blocker recurred for at least three consecutive Goal turns. Tool visibility alone does not activate Goal mode. Never call for ordinary clarification, uncertainty, incomplete work, or recoverable failures.

goal_id.description: The exact goal_id shown in the current active /goal prompt.

reason.description: The specific user or external action required to unblock the goal.

evidence.description: Concrete evidence from the repeated attempts that proves the impasse.

repeated_turns.description: Number of separate turns spent trying to resolve this same blocker.

toolsAdded.name: goal_wait
toolsAdded.description: Keep an active /goal quiet only when the latest effective Goal contract explicitly says Goal mode is active, supplies the matching current goal_id, and progress depends on an arranged external wake event or one safety deadline. Tool visibility alone does not activate Goal mode. Call goal_wait alone. Requests below 10000ms are clamped to 10000ms. Never call for ordinary unfinished work.

goal_id.description: The exact goal_id shown in the current active /goal prompt.

reason.description: Why the goal is waiting and which external event should wake it.

resume_after_ms.description: Optional safety deadline in milliseconds that requests one continuation if no wake message arrives. Values below 10000 are accepted but clamped to 10000.

toolsAdded.name: subagent_gate
toolsAdded.description: Launch generic subagent task slots through pi-subagents RPC v1, require a success quorum, and perform bounded failure-aware retries. Post-launch retries require retrySafety='read-only'; may-write is the safe default.

retrySafety.description: Post-launch retry safety. Defaults to may-write; only read-only tasks may retry automatically after a child starts.

requiredSuccesses.description: Successful task slots required. Defaults to all tasks.

maxAttemptsPerTask.description: Total attempts per task slot, including the first. Defaults to 2.

requireDistinctProviders.description: Count at most one successful task per provider family.

toolsAdded.name: workspace_session_summaries
toolsAdded.description: Show bounded generated summaries from current, connected, and persisted Pi sessions in the same canonical working directory so overlap can be identified before writes.

toolsAdded.name: subagent

With multiple phases, call phase('Exact Title') before each phase's work or set `phase` in the agent options. Use `await workflow(savedName, childArgs)` to run a saved workflow inline; nesting is limited to one level and shares the parent run's concurrency, agent, and token limits. Optional quality helpers include verify(), judgePanel(), loopUntilDry(), and completenessCheck(). Optional control helpers include retry() and gate(); budget exposes total, spent(), and remaining(), and phase('Name', { budget: N }) sets a phase token limit. Use phase('Name'), agent(prompt, opts), parallel(arrayOfFunctions), pipeline(items, ...stages), log(message), args, cwd, process.cwd(), and budget. The workflow must call agent() at least once. parallel() requires functions, not promises, and returns results in input order: await parallel(items.map(item => () => agent(...))). pipeline(items, ...stages) runs stages sequentially for each item while items proceed concurrently; each stage receives (previousValue, originalItem, index).

# Task
# Decision (approved in architecture discussion, 2026-10-31)

Adopt **Option A: an external, versioned artifact store as the runner update channel** — specifically **GitHub Releases** (repo is migrating to github.com/Ewrdad/Kainbain; release assets on a public repo have no bandwidth limit and cost $0) or **Cloudflare R2** (10 GB free, $0 egress) if the S3 API is preferred. **Do NOT** ship runner code from the backend (rejected Option B).

Rationale, tied to the risk register in `docs/../MuseCodeHackathon2026/Portability/RiskAssessment.md`:
- **R05 (backend→runner code execution supply chain)**: the backend already curates prompts/skills that runners execute; if it also distributed runner binaries, one backend compromise = silent RCE on every runner host. Keeping the artifact channel external and signature-verified keeps that blast radius capped.
- **R03 (backend SPOF, accepted)**: pull-based updates keep working while the backend is down.
- **R11 (version/protocol skew)**: backend still does the version handshake at register/heartbeat, shows the fleet version matrix in the UI, flags 'update available', and **refuses dispatch to runners outside the compatibility window** — that enforcement is what actually closes R11.
- **Cost (hobby project, ~10–20 runners, ~50 MB binary × 6 platform artifacts ≈ 300 MB/release, monthly releases, keep 10)**: GitHub Releases = $0 (no bandwidth cap on public repos, Actions free on public repos); R2 = $0 (10 GB free storage, egress always free, reads far under the 10M/mo free Class B); AWS S3 ≈ $0.20/mo but has an egress tail risk ($0.09/GB — a viral burst could be a surprise bill), so avoid raw S3 unless CloudFront (1 TB/mo free) is in front. Signing with minisign/cosign keyless = $0 (one pinned keypair). Option B = $0 external but spends home-upload bandwidth and couples updates to backend uptime.

# What to build (programmatic implementation)

1. **Release pipeline (CI, GitHub Actions — free on public repo)**: on tag `runner-v*`, build runner binaries per platform (linux/darwin/windows × x64/arm64, e.g. Node SEA single executables), produce a `manifest.json` (version, per-asset sha256, release URL, min-compatible-backend), sign the manifest with minisign (or cosign keyless), and attach all artifacts + `manifest.json` + `manifest.json.minisig` to the GitHub Release. Mark canary releases as **pre-release**.
2. **Runner-side update check (pull, on idle)**: runner polls `GET https://api.github.com/repos/Ewrdad/Kainbain/releases/latest` (or `/releases` and pick by semver; skip pre-releases unless opted in) on a jittered interval and when idle between tasks. Compares `tag_name` to its own version; if newer, downloads the matching platform asset + manifest + signature.
3. **Verification before install (mandatory, runner-side)**: verify manifest signature against the **public key pinned in the runner binary** (never fetched from the network), then verify the downloaded asset's sha256 against the manifest. Abort on any mismatch and alert the backend. This keeps R05's runner-side enforcement property: the runner does not trust the backend OR the store blindly — only the pinned key.
4. **Self-update-on-idle**: only swap the binary when the runner has no active task (per MigrationPlan Phase 4 'Runner self-update-on-idle'); download to temp, verify, atomic rename, restart, re-register. Keep the previous binary for one version as a rollback (delete on next successful boot).
5. **Backend coordination (no code transfer)**: on `register`/`heartbeat` the runner reports its version; backend stores it, exposes the fleet version matrix in the Runners settings UI with an 'update available' badge, and **refuses task dispatch to runners below the minimum compatible version** (config knob, e.g. `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_MIN_VERSION`), returning 409 so the runner updates instead of mis-executing.
6. **Rollback**: point the 'latest' pointer back by re-tagging/marking the previous release as latest (GitHub: edit release / delete the bad one so `releases/latest` resolves to the prior tag), or pin `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_PINNED_VERSION` per runner. With R2, versioning is via object versions.
7. **Air-gapped/offline hosts**: support `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_UPDATE_URL` override so the manifest/assets can be mirrored from any S3-compatible store or internal HTTP server.

# Out of scope / rejected
- Backend serving or pushing runner code to runners (Option B) — rejected: maximizes R05 blast radius, couples updates to backend SPOF, costs backend bandwidth. Only niche: the default single-local-runner install can keep updating with the backend container as today; external runners must use the artifact channel.
- Raw AWS S3 without CloudFront — rejected on egress tail-risk/cost grounds for a hobby project.

# Acceptance criteria
- CI publishes a signed runner release on tag; runner on an old version picks it up on idle, verifies signature+sha256, updates, re-registers, and the fleet matrix shows the new version.
- Tampered asset or manifest fails verification and the runner keeps running the old version and alerts.
- Backend refuses dispatch to a below-min-version runner; after updating, dispatch resumes.
- Rollback to the previous release works by reverting the 'latest' pointer.
- Docs updated (PORTABLE_DEPLOYMENT.md / New Runner Onboarding flow) and an ADR added under `adr/`.

# Stage Skills
## question-me
Question rounds are written as append-only JSON blocks to SURVEY.md in the current task's docs/tasks/<taskId>/ folder. Re-read that file before appending so earlier rounds and answers are preserved. Suggested minimum number of questions for this round: 1 (0 = no minimum). Use a distinct outputFile per question stage when a task needs multiple surveys (e.g. FEEDBACK.md, SECURITY_QUESTIONARY.md, INTENT_SURVEY.md).


# Question‑Me (Survey Generator)

Use this skill when you want an **agent stage** to produce a list of multiple‑choice questions (with an optional free‑form notes field) for a human to answer later. The skill:

1. **Generates questions** based on the stage’s prompt.
2. **Writes** a `SURVEY.md` file in the current task’s directory (`docs/tasks/<taskId>/`).
3. **Never overwrites** existing content – it reads the file first and **appends** a new round of questions at the bottom, preserving any prior answers.
4. **Marks the stage as awaiting human input** (task status `waiting_human`) so the UI shows the survey banner and the survey page.
5. Supports **conditional questions** via one simple `showIf` object form: `{ "questionId": "q1", "value": "Option A" }` or `{ "questionId": "q1", "values": ["A", "B"] }`. The UI hides those questions unless the condition is met. No other condition syntax is supported — never write string expressions.
6. **Question ids must be unique across the whole survey** (including every appended round). Re-using an id makes answers ambiguous, so append rounds with fresh ids such as `q5`, `q6`.

## Expected `SURVEY.md` format

The file contains a **machine‑parseable JSON block** wrapped in a fenced code block (`survey-json`). The JSON is the single source of truth; a human‑readable markdown preview is generated from it by the UI.

```markdown
# Survey – generated by the "question‑me" skill

```survey-json
{
  "round": 1,
  "generatedAt": "2026-10-29T13:00:00.000Z",
  "stage": "stage-1792362077711",
  "questions": [
    {
      "id": "q1",
      "type": "single",
      "text": "What is the primary security concern?",
      "options": ["Authentication", "Authorization", "Data protection", "Other"],
      "required": true,
      "showIf": null
    },
    {
      "id": "q2",
      "type": "multiple",
      "text": "Which regulatory frameworks apply?",
      "options": ["PCI‑DSS", "HIPAA", "GDPR", "None"],
      "required": false,
      "showIf": { "questionId": "q1", "value": "Data protection" }
    }
  ],
  "answers": {
    "q1": { "selected": ["Data protection"], "notes": "PII in uploads" }
  }
}
```

*The UI renders each question as a set of radio‑buttons or check‑boxes with a **Notes** textarea underneath. Fill `generatedAt` with the current UTC time in ISO‑8601 (as above) and `stage` with the stage id already resolved into this prompt (`stage-1792362077711`) — never leave a placeholder token in the written file; the backend validates the round and rejects unreadable ones.*

When the user finishes the survey, the UI updates the `answers` object in‑place (preserving the surrounding JSON) and saves the file.

### Append‑only behaviour
- If `SURVEY.md` already exists, the skill **reads** it, determines the next `round` number, and **appends** a new JSON block under a new heading `## Round N`.
- Existing `answers` objects are left untouched.
- The skill must never delete or rewrite previous rounds.

## How the engine treats the skill
- During stage execution, after the agent returns **success**, the backend inspects the stage’s skill list. If `question-me` is present, it reads `SURVEY.md` and decides:
  - **Unanswered required questions** (or no `SURVEY.md` at all) → the task parks with status `waiting_human` instead of auto‑advancing. The task detail page shows the survey banner; the survey page opens at `/tasks/:taskId/survey`.
  - **Explicitly empty round** (`questions: []` — you had good reason to ask nothing) → the run advances normally, no parking.
  - **Already answered** → the run advances normally.
- Submitting the survey (`POST /tasks/:taskId/survey`) merges answers only — questions are never added, removed, or renamed there. A partial save stays parked; a complete submit advances the task to its next stage, which may then read `SURVEY.md`.

## Downstream stages
Tell the stage after the survey (e.g. the plan stage) to factor in `SURVEY.md` — for example: "Factor in SURVEY.md into your plan. If there is not enough information, fail the stage with information needed." A failback re-runs the question stage, which appends a fresh round at the bottom.

## Human‑only edge‑cases
- If you genuinely have **no questions**, still write one round with `questions: []` rather than writing no file. An empty round advances without parking; a missing file parks so a human confirms there is nothing to ask (the survey page offers Continue in both cases).

## UI considerations (mobile & desktop)
- Render each question inside a `<fieldset>`.
- Options are full‑width touch targets; use `type="radio"` for `single` and `type="checkbox"` for `multiple`.
- The **Notes** textarea is optional but always present; on mobile it expands to the full width.
- Conditional visibility is evaluated client‑side; hidden questions are collapsed but their stored answers remain unchanged.
- Accessibility: all inputs have `aria‑label` and are keyboard‑navigable.

## Configuring the output file

The output file name is read from the skill configuration. In `KB_config.json`:

```json
{
  "keywords": {
    "outputFile": { "value": "SURVEY.md" },
    "minQuestions": { "value": "0" }
  },
  "defaults": { "mode": "direct" }
}
```

A stage attachment can override the file name without editing the skill, for
example:

```json
{ "name": "question-me", "config": { "outputFile": "FEEDBACK.md" } }
```

Accepted config keys (canonical first, then aliases): `outputFile`, `surveyFile`,
`surveyFileName`, `fileName`, `targetFile`, `file`. Plain names without an
extension become a `.md` file (`FEEDBACK` → `FEEDBACK.md`); anything else must
already end in `.md`. Path traversal or unsafe names fall back to `SURVEY.md`.

Multi-stage tasks should give each question stage its own file, e.g.
`FEEDBACK.md`, `SECURITY_QUESTIONARY.md`, `INTENT_SURVEY.md`, while the
default single-survey setup keeps `SURVEY.md`.

## Suggested minimum question count

`minQuestions` is a soft prompt hint only; the engine never enforces it. A value
of `0` disables the suggestion.

## Minimal `KB_config.json`
The skill defaults to `SURVEY.md` and a disabled minimum, so an empty object is
still sufficient (`{}`).

# Stage Verdict (KainBain)

KainBain decides whether this stage passed from your output. End your final
message with exactly one verdict block (no code fence around it):

KAINBAIN_VERDICT: PASS

or, when the stage must NOT pass:

KAINBAIN_VERDICT: FAIL
KAINBAIN_REASON: <what is wrong, concretely — file, test, behaviour>
KAINBAIN_FIX: <how the next attempt should fix it — what to change, run, or check>

**Important:** The verdict block must be plain text. Do NOT surround it with triple backticks, quote blocks, or any other formatting. The engine only recognizes lines that start with `KAINBAIN_VERDICT:`, `KAINBAIN_REASON:`, or `KAINBAIN_FIX:` (case-insensitive) followed by a colon.

Rules:

- **Agent stages only.** A verdict is optional guidance for AGENT stages.
  Human checkpoints (including legacy `review`), CI stages (including legacy
  `script` and the removed `deploy` type), and merge stages never render,
  require, or are failed by a verdict — the engine ignores any verdict block
  in their output. Never instruct a human or CI stage to produce one.
- Before the verdict block, write a short summary (2–5 sentences) of what you
  did and which files you changed.
- If a stage fails, put the reasoning in the FAIL block's reason and fix
  lines — the engine preserves your final message in the failure report
  (`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`) for the next attempt. Do not
  hand-write a separate failure file; the engine is the single writer.
- If this session offers a `Fail_stage_skill` (or `fail_stage`) tool, calling
  it is the primary fail path — still end with the FAIL block too.
- On wrapped harnesses (muse, antigravity, custom command, opencode) there is
  no such tool: the FAIL block is the ONLY fail signal. Prose verdicts
  ("Verdict: FAIL", "Stage failed") anywhere else are ignored by the engine.
- A FAIL block is honoured only with BOTH reason and fix guidance non-empty.
  KainBain never fails a stage without guidance to fix: a reasonless FAIL is
  treated as a pass and flagged for human review instead.
- Do NOT request or specify a target stage — KainBain routes the task back to
  the stage configured for failback on this stage.

# Risk Assessment — New Portable Architecture (Runner Paradigm)

> **Scope:** [NewArchitecture.md](NewArchitecture.md) + `NewArchitecture.excalidraw` (2026-10-25), assessed against [EscalationLadder.md](~/projects/kainbain/docs/Reliability&Risk/EscalationLadder.md), [HandNotesOnParallelism.md](~/projects/kainbain/docs/MuseCodeHackathon2026/HandNotesOnParallelism.md), [MuseIntegrationSpike.md](~/projects/kainbain/docs/MuseCodeHackathon2026/MuseIntegrationSpike.md), [Deliverables.md](~/projects/kainbain/docs/MuseCodeHackathon2026/Deliverables.md), `KB Architecture.md`, `PORTABLE_DEPLOYMENT.md`, `Disaster Model Plan.md`, ADRs 0001–0007, and the risk template in `Reliability&Risk/RiskRegister/Template.md`.
> **Status:** Replaces the 2026-10-25 first-pass assessment (see §2 for the critique of that pass). Draft for decision, not yet accepted.
> **Method:** Template scoring — Impact = max(C, I, A) on 1–4, Likelihood 1–4, Score = Impact × Likelihood (1–16). Every risk also carries a **residual score**: the score that remains *if* its stated Prevention is actually built and tested. Likelihood means "likelihood if shipped exactly as documented today," not likelihood in the current single-process system.

---

## 1. Executive summary

The proposal splits one supervised process into three trust and failure domains: a Docker-Compose frontend, a Docker-Compose backend ("Engine": prompt curation, queue, project/task state, runner gateway), and N native Runner binaries that discover local harnesses, clone repos, create git worktrees, run harness sessions, and commit/push. The default install (backend + frontend + one local Runner) must reproduce today's behaviour exactly.

**Verdict: direction is sound, design is not yet buildable as specified. Overall inherent risk HIGH; residual risk MEDIUM if — and only if — the Phase gates in §7 are treated as blocking.**

Three judgements drive everything below:

1. **The two correct calls are already made.** Runners native (harness CLIs, git auth, worktree I/O do not containerise faithfully) and repo-as-source-of-truth retained. Neither should be re-litigated.
2. **The document names its dangers but specifies none of the mechanisms that retire them.** Authentication, mutual exclusion, failure detection, capability routing, push/report ordering, and version compatibility are all "need to explore." In a single-process system these are internal invariants the runtime enforces for free; in this design each becomes a protocol that must be designed, versioned, and tested. That gap — not any single bug — is the risk.
3. **The escalation ladder is the sharpest lens on the cost.** Distribution does not just add failure modes; it *reprices recovery*. Steps 1–3 (scripted retry, agent-led recovery, interrupt/resume) are cheap today because one supervisor owns the session, the queue, and the filesystem. Split across processes and hosts, the same faults land at steps 5–7 unless lease/fencing, heartbeat, and idempotent completion are built *first*. §5 quantifies this shift; §6 assigns every ladder step an owner.

**Recommendation:** strangler migration, four gated phases (§7). Do not build multi-Runner until single-Runner-over-the-wire has proven parity. The first phase (containerise, keep the embedded runner) captures most of the portability deliverable at a fraction of the risk and should be shippable on its own.

### Risk register at a glance (inherent → residual)

| # | Risk | Score | Residual | Ladder start (unmitigated → mitigated) |
|---|------|-------|----------|----------------------------------------|
| R01 | Double-claim and unfenced git push | 12 | 4 | 5 → 1 |
| R02 | Repo-as-truth consistency: dual writers, push/report ordering | 12 | 6 | 5 → 3 |
| R03 | Backend SPOF and single-writer bottleneck | 12 | 8 | 7 → 7 |
| R04 | Unauthenticated Runner→Backend channel | 12 | 4 | 9 → 1 |
| R05 | Backend→Runner code execution and prompt/skill supply chain | 12 | 8 | 9 → 6 |
| R06 | Escalation-ladder repricing / recovery-ownership vacuum | 12 | 6 | 5 → 3 |
| R07 | Capability and alias misrouting (incl. harness version drift) | 12 | 4 | 4 → 1 |
| R08 | Partition, zombie Runner, and lost mid-stage work | 9 | 6 | 3 → 3 |
| R09 | Secrets and git-credential sprawl; loss of attribution | 9 | 6 | 9 → 6 |
| R10 | Git worktree, clone, and disk contention; cleanup races | 9 | 4 | 3 → 1 |
| R11 | Version and protocol skew (backend / Runner / harness) | 9 | 6 | 7 → 6 |
| R12 | UI concurrency; steering and approval misrouting | 9 | 6 | 6 → 1 |
| R13 | Cost, quota, and compute runaway; priority starvation | 9 | 6 | 6 → 1 |
| R14 | Observability fragmentation; log ordering and completeness | 8 | 4 | 6 → 1 |
| R15 | Portability regressions defeat the portability goal | 6 | 4 | 1 → 1 |
| R16 | Migration, cutover, and rollback failure | 6 | 3 | 8 → 3 |

Residual scores assume the Prevention in each section is implemented *and covered by the named test*. A mitigation that exists only as prose earns no residual credit.

---

## 2. Critique of the first-pass assessment (what this document fixes)

The first pass (805 lines, 12 risks) was a good launching point: it found the right headline risks (SPOF, locking, auth, ladder shift, alias routing, worktrees), used the project template, and recommended a phased strangler. It is replaced, not patched, because of the following defects:

1. **Score inflation destroyed prioritisation.** Four risks scored 12 and one scored 16, with Likelihood 4 ("almost certain") asserted for seven risks without evidence. When everything is Likelihood 4, nothing is. R01's 16 required both Impact 4 *and* Likelihood 4 for a backend that is already a single point of failure today — it scored the *pre-existing* condition, not the *delta* this architecture introduces. This pass separates inherent delta from pre-existing exposure and cuts unjustified 4s.
2. **It treated a lease as a lock.** Its R02 fix ("claim returns a lease; Runner must hold lease to push") does not fence the actual write: the Runner pushes to the git remote directly, and a partitioned "zombie" Runner whose lease expired can still push after a second Runner has completed the task. A lease without a fencing token checked *at push/completion time* is advisory. Corrected in R01/R02/R08.
3. **It modelled trust in only one direction.** It covered rogue Runners attacking the backend, but not the reverse — and the reverse is the larger blast radius. The backend ships curated prompts and skill bodies to Runners that execute harness sessions (per the Muse spike, under an operator-chosen allow-all/YOLO posture). A compromised backend, or prompt injection from untrusted repo/task content, is remote code execution on *every* Runner host. Added as R05.
4. **It missed the second source of truth.** "Repo as source of truth" plus "Runner pushes to origin" plus "backend writes task/project files" is three writers with no stated transaction or ordering between *push succeeded* and *completion reported*. The first pass praised the invariant without stress-testing it. Added as R02.
5. **One ladder step per risk, presented as a property of the risk.** In reality the ladder start depends on which mitigations exist (its own text admitted this for R02/R03, then still printed a single number in the summary table, where it will be quoted out of context). This pass prints unmitigated → mitigated pairs everywhere.
6. **Missing risk classes entirely:** cost/quota runaway and priority starvation under parallel burn (the ladder's second goal is explicitly *minimise token burn*, yet the first pass never scored the risk that most directly attacks it); migration/cutover/rollback; harness *version* drift within "capability" (a Runner "has Muse" at the wrong version is not capable); steering/approval delivery to a specific live session; and the self-defeating risk that install complexity kills the portability deliverable it exists to serve. Added as R12–R16.
7. **Unverifiable specificity.** It cited precise internals (function names, test files, line-level behaviours) as load-bearing evidence for scores without distinguishing "verified in the cited doc" from "plausible inference." This pass keeps citations at the level of the documents actually in scope and flags inferences as inferences.
8. **Recommendations had no exit criteria.** "Implement lease/claim" is a task, not a gate. §7 restates the phases with pass/fail exit criteria and explicit kill criteria, so a phase cannot be declared done on enthusiasm.

What is deliberately retained: the CIA template, the ladder framing, the phased strangler recommendation, and the per-risk Prevention/Detection/Response shape. The first pass structured the problem well; it scored and closed it too optimistically.

---

## 3. Threat model and trust boundaries (new — absent from both prior docs)

Actors and what they can do if the channel is built as currently specified ("register, request task, receive prompt, push, report complete"):

| Actor | Reach today (as specified) | Boundary that must exist |
|-------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| Rogue host on the network | Register as a Runner, claim tasks, receive prompts/skills, push commits | Authenticated, approved, project-scoped Runner identity (R04) |
| Compromised / malicious Runner | Exfiltrate task content, push arbitrary commits, hold leases hostage, burn quota | Least-privilege scope, revocable identity, push fencing, per-Runner budget (R01, R04, R13) |
| Compromised backend | Execute arbitrary harness sessions on every Runner host | Runner-side execution policy: project allowlist enforced *by the Runner*, skill/prompt provenance, sandbox posture (R05) |
| Untrusted repo / task content | Prompt-inject the agent via task text, repo files, skills | Treat all task/repo content as untrusted input to an executor; curated-prompt boundary documented (R05) |
| Honest-but-dead Runner | Stall a task indefinitely; push late after re-dispatch | Lease + heartbeat + fencing token (R01, R08) |
| Honest-but-old Runner | Mis-execute new stage shapes silently | Version handshake, protocol versioning (R11) |
| Operator error | Duplicate tasks from a desynced UI; steer the wrong session | Backend-authoritative UI, ownership-routed steering (R12) |

Two properties follow. First, **the Runner is an executor, not a client**: any design review that treats it as a thin API consumer will under-secure it. Second, **git is part of the trusted computing base**: whoever can push can land code that later stages execute. Backend-side checks that are not also enforced at push/completion time do not exist as far as the remote is concerned.

---

## 4. Decisions that must be taken before build (decision register)

These are not risks; they are unspecified decisions that *generate* risks. Each blocks the phase noted. Leaving any of them "to explore" during implementation converts a design decision into an emergent behaviour.

| ID | Decision | Options (summary) | Blocks |
|----|----------|-------------------|--------|
| D1 | Mutual exclusion | Backend lease + fencing token vs static sharding | Phase 2 |
| D2 | Completion atomicity | Push-then-report with idempotent reconciliation vs backend-mediated push | Phase 2 |
| D3 | Alias routing authority | Backend-routed (Runner advertises capability) vs Runner-routed | Phase 2 |
| D4 | Runner identity | Per-Runner token + human approval vs shared secret vs mTLS | Phase 2 (remote: Phase 3) |
| D5 | Session ownership | Steering/approval/pause routed via backend to owning Runner; behaviour when owner is offline | Phase 3 |
| D6 | Source-of-truth reconciliation | When backend re-reads repo state after a Runner push; cache invalidation rule | Phase 2 |
| D7 | Protocol versioning | Versioned Runner API + compatibility window + upgrade policy | Phase 2 |
| D8 | Global budget authority | Who can stop parallel burn: per-Runner, per-project, global caps | Phase 3 |
| D9 | Runner-side execution policy | Allowlist, skill provenance, sandbox/YOLO posture per Runner | Phase 3 |
| D10 | State ownership split | Diagram shows "Mounted Projects folder" (backend) *and* "Loaded Projects" per Runner: which writes win, and how do they converge? | Phase 1 |

D10 deserves emphasis: the Excalidraw diagram and the lifecycle text do not currently agree on a single-writer story for project/task state. Resolving D10 on paper is the cheapest risk reduction available in the whole programme.

---

## 5. Escalation-ladder analysis

The ladder (cheapest first): **1** scripted in-task recovery → **2** agent-led recovery → **3** interrupt/resume → **4** retry stage → **5** fail back to earlier stage → **6** request human, keep running → **7** halt task, keep others → **8** halt all, restart → **9** halt all, wait for human. Its stated goals, in order: minimise human intervention, minimise token burn, then prevent misaligned behaviour / wasted compute / network exposure.

### How distribution reprices each step

| Step | Today (single process) | As proposed (unmitigated) | Mechanism of the shift |
|------|------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|
| 1 Scripted | Default path; supervisor retries in-process | Must be re-implemented identically in every Runner, on every OS | No shared supervisor; correctness is now N implementations |
| 2 Agent-led | Agent sees engine-surfaced errors | Roughly unchanged | Agent still co-located with its harness session |
| 3 Interrupt/resume | `session/resume` against a live supervised host | Session dies with its Runner; "resume" becomes re-dispatch and loses mid-stage context | Session ownership moved to the least reliable component |
| 4 Retry stage | Re-queue locally | Works, but costs a full re-claim + re-clone/pull cycle | Retry is now network- and git-priced |
| 5 Fail back | Rare | More frequent: push conflicts, capability rejects, divergent stage history | Every cross-Runner race resolves here |
| 6 Request human | Rare | More frequent: version skew, log gaps, stale credentials, budget trips | Heterogeneity surfaces as operator work |
| 7 Halt task | Rare | Backend stalls and zombie tasks land here by default | No failure detector specified |
| 8 Halt all / restart | Very rare | The only specified remedy for backend failure | SPOF with no failover story |
| 9 Halt all / wait | Very rare | New realistic class: auth bypass, credential leak, supply-chain execution | Trust boundaries that did not exist before |

**Net effect:** unmitigated, mean-time-to-human-intervention falls and expected token burn per completed task rises (re-dispatch restarts stages from scratch; failback loops across Runners can re-burn the same stage repeatedly). That is a direct regression against the ladder's two primary goals, and it should be stated that plainly in any go/no-go decision.

### Ladder-ownership matrix (the artefact R06 requires)

| Step | Owner after distribution | Signal that triggers it |
|------|--------------------------|-------------------------|
| 1 | Runner (harness-local retry) + Backend (claim retry, backoff) | Harness error; claim conflict (409) |
| 2 | Runner (in-session agent) | Agent-observable failure mid-run |
| 3 | Backend (lease expiry → re-dispatch) | Heartbeat missed beyond lease TTL |
| 4 | Backend (stage reset, new claim) | Runner reports stage unrecoverable |
| 5 | Backend (workflow regression) | Push/fencing conflict; stage verdict fail |
| 6 | Backend → UI (request, keep running) | Budget threshold; reliability threshold; log gap |
| 7 | Backend → UI (halt one task) | Retry exhaustion; unresolvable git state |
| 8 | Operator (restart/redeploy backend) | Backend health failure |
| 9 | Operator (security incident) | Auth bypass; credential leak; malicious push |

No ladder step may have two owners or none. Any failure mode that cannot be placed in this table is an unspecified recovery, and unspecified recoveries default to step 9 in practice — a human noticing.

---

## 6. Detailed risks

### R01 — Double-claim and unfenced git push

**Score: 12 (C1 · I3 · A2 × L4) → Residual: 4**

Two Runners polling the same queue *will* eventually claim the same task if claiming is not atomic — the architecture doc concedes the mechanism is unexplored. The subtler failure survives the obvious fix: Runner A is partitioned, its lease expires, Runner B completes the task, then A reconnects and pushes. A backend lease does not fence a direct `git push`; the remote accepts A's late, divergent history. Consequences: competing worktrees and commits, a failed or forced push, and stage history recording two contradictory outcomes for one execution.

- **Prevention:** atomic claim (`POST /tasks/:id/claim` → 200 + lease or 409); every claim carries a monotonically increasing **fencing token / execution epoch**; completion and any backend-mediated acceptance check the token, and the push path must be fenced too — either backend-mediated push, or a pre-receive check / branch naming that encodes the epoch so a stale Runner's push is rejected by construction. Idempotent completion keyed by a stable execution ID so a retried report is a no-op, not a duplicate.
- **Detection:** claim-conflict rate (any sustained non-zero rate outside deploys is a defect); rejected stale-epoch pushes; divergent stage-history check on completion.
- **Response:** losing execution's worktree is discarded; if a stale push landed, fail the task back for reconciliation (step 5) — never silent force-push.
- **Ladder start: 5 → 1.** Unmitigated, reconciliation needs an earlier stage; with claim + fencing, a conflict is a scripted 409/backoff, invisible to the user.
- **Test that earns the residual:** two Runners, one task, forced partition of the first mid-stage; assert exactly one completion is accepted and the stale push is rejected.

### R02 — Repo-as-truth consistency: dual writers, push/report ordering

**Score: 12 (C1 · I4 · A2 × L3) → Residual: 6**

The retained invariant — repo is source of truth, database is cache only — was safe when one process wrote the files. The proposal creates three writers (backend task/project files, Runner git operations, the git remote) and specifies no ordering between "push succeeded" and "completion reported," nor when the backend re-reads repo state after a push. Both orderings fail differently: report-then-push-crash leaves the backend believing work exists that the repo lacks; push-then-report-crash leaves repo work the backend will re-dispatch and duplicate. The diagram's "Mounted Projects folder" (backend) alongside per-Runner "Loaded Projects" (D10) makes the write-ownership question concrete and currently unanswered.

- **Prevention:** decide D2/D6/D10 explicitly. Completion must be reconcilable from the repo alone: the completion report references the pushed commit SHA, the backend verifies that SHA is reachable before marking the stage complete, and a boot/periodic reconciler repairs report/push divergence in either direction.
- **Detection:** reconciler divergence counter; "completed stage with unreachable SHA" must be a pageable-zero metric.
- **Response:** divergence → stage returns to interrupted (step 3) for re-dispatch or reconciliation, not to a human with a corrupted history.
- **Ladder start: 5 → 3.**

### R03 — Backend single point of failure and single-writer bottleneck

**Score: 12 (C2 · I4 · A4 × L3) → Residual: 8**

Every Runner polls, reports, and pushes metadata through one backend, which is also sole writer of queue and task state and sole server to the UI. Backend down means all Runners idle and the board empty; backend degraded means the queue degrades for everyone at once. Note the honest scoping the first pass missed: this is largely a *pre-existing* condition, not a new one. The delta this architecture adds is blast radius (N Runners' in-flight work now depends on it) and contention (N pollers/reporters against a write path designed for one process). It is scored on that delta, hence Likelihood 3, not 4.

- **Prevention:** durable queue/lease state (no in-memory-only dispatch state); atomic file writes; poll backpressure (long-poll or push with jittered backoff — N Runners must not be able to DDoS their own engine, especially in a thundering herd after a backend restart); a documented consistency model instead of "keep an eye on it."
- **Detection:** health endpoint exposing queue depth, dispatch latency, connected/idle Runner counts; alert on oldest-waiting-task age, not just up/down.
- **Response:** restart with transactional recovery that re-queues in-flight work as *interrupted*, never as *failed* and never as *complete*.
- **Ladder start: 7 → 7.** This is the one risk mitigations do not cheapen: a dead backend halts tasks until it returns (step 8 in the common case). The residual stays high deliberately — the honest mitigation is accepting and documenting it for current scale, with the consistency design kept replica-ready.

### R04 — Unauthenticated Runner→Backend channel

**Score: 12 (C4 · I4 · A3 × L3) → Residual: 4**

"Implement some sort of easy authentication" is currently the entire specification for a channel that hands out curated prompts, receives stage completions, and — via pushes — lands executable code. Any host that can reach the backend can register, claim work, exfiltrate task/skill content, and push commits that later stages execute. Likelihood is conditional and stated honestly: negligible on a loopback-only default install, high the moment a remote Runner is permitted — which is the stated purpose of the design.

- **Prevention:** per-Runner cryptographic identity issued at registration, human-approved (UI/CLI), project-scoped, revocable and rotatable; backend loopback-only by default with remote access an explicit, authenticated opt-in; least-privilege scopes (claim/report only for allowlisted projects).
- **Detection:** audit log keyed by Runner identity on every claim/report/push; alert on unknown identity or one identity appearing from multiple origins.
- **Response:** revoke identity → leases expire → work re-queues. A landed malicious push is a security incident (step 9), not a retry.
- **Ladder start: 9 → 1.** Mitigated, a bad request is a logged rejection; unmitigated, it is halt-everything.
- **Test that earns the residual:** unauthenticated and wrongly-scoped requests to every Runner endpoint are rejected; a revoked Runner cannot claim, report, or complete.

### R05 — Backend→Runner code execution and prompt/skill supply chain

**Score: 12 (C4 · I4 · A2 × L3) → Residual: 8**

The direction the first pass missed. The backend curates prompts and skills and dispatches them to Runners that run harness sessions with broad host permissions (the Muse integration operates under an operator-chosen allow-all posture, with repo/task content flowing into prompts). Whoever or whatever controls prompt/skill content — a compromised backend, a malicious project, an injected skill, hostile task text — gets execution on every Runner host, under that host's "Local git auth" (per the diagram). Parallelism multiplies this from one host to the fleet.

- **Prevention:** Runner-side execution policy that does not trust the backend blindly: per-Runner project allowlist *enforced by the Runner*, documented sandbox/approval posture per Runner (with the permissive mode an explicit per-Runner opt-in, never a fleet default), skill provenance (only backend-signed or locally pinned skills execute), and task/repo content explicitly classified as untrusted input in the prompt-curation boundary.
- **Detection:** Runner logs the provenance of every prompt/skill it executes; backend records which skill versions were dispatched to which Runner.
- **Response:** suspect dispatch → halt fleet execution pending human review (step 9 for confirmed compromise; step 6 for suspicion).
- **Ladder start: 9 → 6.** Residual stays elevated: mitigations shrink the surface but an executor fleet is inherently high-impact. This risk, not R03's, is the ceiling on how casually remote Runners should be added.

# ADR 0009 — Runner↔Backend protocol sketch (v1)

**Status:** Accepted (MigrationPlan Phase 0 gate, 2026-10-26)
**Date:** 2026-10-26
**Task:** MigrationPlan Phase 0 (paper only; no code in this ADR)
**Decides:** the wire shape Phase 2 builds. Wire format is JSON over HTTPS
(same shapes over loopback HTTP for the default install); log frames stream
over the existing WebSocket channel pattern (`/ws`), sequenced per
execution.

## Context

RiskAssessment R01/R04/R07/R11/R14 turn today's in-process calls
(`agentRunner` → `SessionStore` → harness registry) into a protocol that must
be authenticated, versioned, fenced, and observable. This sketch fixes the
message set and the rules; Phase 2 assigns exact paths/status codes and the
conformance tests.

## Decision

Lifecycle, in order:

1. `register` — Runner presents: Runner id (stable per host, generated at
   install), human-approved join token (D4), host facts (OS, working dirs),
   discovered harnesses with versions, runnable models, permitted YOLO tiers
   (D9), disk headroom. Backend answers `pending` (awaits UI approve/deny per
   the onboarding flow) or `active` + per-Runner credential + protocol
   version. Unknown identity or wrong scope is rejected on every endpoint
   (R04 test: unauthenticated / wrong-scope / revoked Runner rejected
   everywhere).
2. `heartbeat` (interval, backend-side expiry) — refreshes capabilities,
   tier ceiling, disk headroom, project allowlist digest, and all three
   version axes (backend, Runner, per-harness versions; D7). Stale
   capability expires: no dispatch against a heartbeat older than the TTL.
   Heartbeat also carries harness-change detection (a harness whose version
   moved is re-advertised, never silently kept).
3. `claim` — `POST /tasks/:id/claim` → `200` + lease `{ executionId,
   epoch }` or `409` + holder epoch. The epoch is the fencing token (D1):
   backend-issued, monotonic, never wall-clock. One task, one holder.
4. `progress` — stage lifecycle events keyed by `executionId`; idempotent
   ingestion (a retried report is a no-op, not a duplicate stage).
5. `log ingest` — sequenced frames `{ executionId, seq, bytes }`; the
   backend assigns canonical ordering and validates/dedupes on ingest
   (execution ID + sequence). The Runner keeps a local spill file replayed
   after a crash. Gaps are represented in the data ("logs truncated —
   Runner disconnected"), never papered over (R14).
6. `complete` / `error` — references the pushed commit SHA (remote-backed,
   transport row 1) or branch + SHA presence (grandfathered local-only, row
   2). The backend verifies reachability/presence (D2/D6) before marking
   complete; a stale epoch's push is rejected by construction (D1) and the
   stage returns to `interrupted` for re-dispatch, never silent force-push.
7. `load` / project sync — backend tells the Runner to load a repo;
   remote-backed clones from origin then pulls; grandfathered local-only
   adopts/shares the path (no clone-from-origin, no push). A Runner
   advertises no capability for a repo it cannot fetch (transport row 3).

Onboarding handshake (unchanged from the onboarding flow): Runner boots with
env-pointed backend → optional backend-identity check → join request with
host/harness facts → user approves/denies in Settings → automatic secure
channel. Minimal approval UI (pending join requests, approve/deny) ships in
Phase 2; the full Runners config screen is Phase 3.

Versioning: `protocol: "v1"` on every message; compatibility window N-1
minor (D7). Outside-window Runners idle with an explicit operator signal
(step 6), never best-effort dispatch. Frontend↔backend stays lockstep (one
Compose release pins both; backend version on `/status`, mismatch banner in
the UI — Phase 1).

Error vocabulary reuses the existing contract style: unsupported capability
answers `501 { code }`, unknown session entries `404 { code }` (per the
harness-contract precedent in `api/agent/harnessContract.js`), auth failures
`401/403` with revocation taking effect at the next heartbeat at the latest
(leases expire; work re-queues).

Rejected: backend-mediated push (D2 rejects — backend never touches git
remotes); Runner-to-UI channel (D5 — the backend is the UI's only source of
truth); timestamp leases (clock skew); unsequenced log append (misordering
under retry is guaranteed, not hypothetical).

## Consequences

- Phase 2 implements exactly this message set; anything not here (impromptu
  read-only requests, T0-only, remote onboarding) waits for Phase 3.
- The partition test (two Runners, one task, first partitioned mid-stage →
  exactly one completion accepted, stale push rejected) is the test that
  earns the residual on R01; the auth matrix earns R04; the version-skew
  fleet earns R11.

## Verification map

Paper phase: verified by review against D1/D2/D4/D6/D7/D9/D14 in ADR 0005.
Code-phase hooks: claim-fencing tests, reconciler divergence counter
(pageable-zero), ingest validation errors, fleet version matrix in the UI.

Rationale, tied to the risk register in `docs/../MuseCodeHackathon2026/Portability/RiskAssessment.md`:
- **R05 (backend→runner code execution supply chain)**: the backend already curates prompts/skills that runners execute; if it also distributed runner binaries, one backend compromise = silent RCE on every runner host. Keeping the artifact channel external and signature-verified keeps that blast radius capped.
- **R03 (backend SPOF, accepted)**: pull-based updates keep working while the backend is down.
- **R11 (version/protocol skew)**: backend still does the version handshake at register/heartbeat, shows the fleet version matrix in the UI, flags 'update available', and **refuses dispatch to runners outside the compatibility window** — that enforcement is what actually closes R11.
- **Cost (hobby project, ~10–20 runners, ~50 MB binary × 6 platform artifacts ≈ 300 MB/release, monthly releases, keep 10)**: GitHub Releases = $0 (no bandwidth cap on public repos, Actions free on public repos); R2 = $0 (10 GB free storage, egress always free, reads far under the 10M/mo free Class B); AWS S3 ≈ $0.20/mo but has an egress tail risk ($0.09/GB — a viral burst could be a surprise bill), so avoid raw S3 unless CloudFront (1 TB/mo free) is in front. Signing with minisign/cosign keyless = $0 (one pinned keypair). Option B = $0 external but spends home-upload bandwidth and couples updates to backend uptime.

# What to build (programmatic implementation)

1. **Release pipeline (CI, GitHub Actions — free on public repo)**: on tag `runner-v*`, build runner binaries per platform (linux/darwin/windows × x64/arm64, e.g. Node SEA single executables), produce a `manifest.json` (version, per-asset sha256, release URL, min-compatible-backend), sign the manifest with minisign (or cosign keyless), and attach all artifacts + `manifest.json` + `manifest.json.minisig` to the GitHub Release. Mark canary releases as **pre-release**.
2. **Runner-side update check (pull, on idle)**: runner polls `GET https://api.github.com/repos/Ewrdad/Kainbain/releases/latest` (or `/releases` and pick by semver; skip pre-releases unless opted in) on a jittered interval and when idle between tasks. 3. **Never overwrites** existing content – it reads the file first and **appends** a new round of questions at the bottom, preserving any prior answers.
4. **Marks the stage as awaiting human input** (task status `waiting_human`) so the UI shows the survey banner and the survey page.
